# Architect / Coder / Tester Loop

Three roles, one task at a time: **architect** writes the spec, **coder** implements it, **tester**
verifies it independently. The roles are not a naming convention — they are enforced by what each one
is permitted to touch.

## Separation by capability, not by instruction

Each subagent definition in [[stickfps]] carries an explicit tool grant, and the grants are the
mechanism:

- **architect** — Read, Grep, Glob, Write, Edit, but **barred from `/src`**. It can write specs and
  cannot write code.
- **coder** — the same plus Bash. It can build and run.
- **tester** — **no Write and no Edit at all**, deliberately.

> "Never let the tester subagent edit files, and never let the architect subagent touch application
> source — that separation is what keeps this loop honest."
> — browser_game_stickfps/.tooling/commands/game-loop.md, 2026-07-25

The reasoning generalises past agents entirely. A verifier that can edit will, under pressure, make
the failure go away rather than report it — the same reason a test author who can change the assertion
tends to. Removing the capability removes the temptation, and it is enforceable, which an instruction
is not.

## The orchestration loop

`/game-loop` runs: spec → implement → verify, with four rules worth extracting.

1. **Max 3 fix attempts** per task, then stop. A three-strike rule converts "keep trying" into an
   explicit hand-back to a human, which is the point at which someone re-reads the spec instead of
   the code.
2. **Stop and ask on any "Open Questions" in the spec.** Uncertainty halts the loop rather than
   getting resolved by guess — see [[spec-driven-development]].
3. **On PASS**: tick the `TASKS.md` box, log to `PROGRESS.md`, commit.
4. **Every third task, rewrite the state summary** "in under 300 tokens" so the working state
   survives a context compaction. This is the interesting one: it treats context as a resource with a
   budget and schedules maintenance of it, rather than discovering it is gone.

## Where it was not followed

Step 3's commit instruction was not obeyed — [[stickfps]] has 9 commits for 11 rounds of work, made
in one 7-hour import session, and `PROGRESS.md` twice records "No commit made (user hasn't asked)".
The logging half of step 3 *was* followed rigorously, which is why
[[progress-md-as-build-log]] exists at all and why the git history is not the working record. See
[[import-finished-work-into-git]].

The four `.tooling` files also still name the retired transport and host — [[documentation-drift]].

## Confidence

`confidence: medium`. The definitions and the loop are directly evidenced and the outputs (9 specs,
11 logged rounds) are consistent with them, but the pattern is observed in **one repository**, so it
is not yet established as a recurring habit.
